canonicalExplanation.summary: **CMake** describes a C++ build as **targets**: libraries and executables, each with its own sources, include directories, compile features and links. Modern CMake sets options **per target** (`target_compile_features`, `target_compile_options`, `target_link_libraries`), not with global variables like `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS` edited everywhere. It tracks **header dependencies** automatically, so changing a header rebuilds every file that includes it. Keep the whole program on **one language standard and consistent flags**: object files built with different standards or incompatible flags can disagree about class layouts and break the ODR, even when the linker happily accepts them.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner builds their library with -std=c++17 and their app with -std=c++20 and a different define, compiling some objects by hand. Everything links, then a std::string member reads garbage at run time. A changed class header recompiles every dependent translation unit before tests link against one consistent layout. In this lesson you'll configure and build a multi-target CMake project without global mutable build settings.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Conceptual constraints and diagnostics**, **Exceptions and guarantees**, **Headers and source separation** and **Compile and link model**.

sections.heading: The model: targets with their own settings
sections.body:
```cmake
# CMakeLists.txt
cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.20)
project(orders LANGUAGES CXX)

add_library(orders_core src/parse.cpp src/order.cpp)
target_include_directories(orders_core PUBLIC include)      # users get include/ too.
target_compile_features(orders_core PUBLIC cxx_std_20)      # one standard, propagated.
target_compile_options(orders_core PRIVATE -Wall -Wextra)   # only this target's own files.

add_executable(orders_app src/main.cpp)
target_link_libraries(orders_app PRIVATE orders_core)       # inherits PUBLIC settings.

enable_testing()
add_executable(orders_tests tests/test_parse.cpp)
target_link_libraries(orders_tests PRIVATE orders_core)
add_test(NAME parse COMMAND orders_tests)
```

```bash
cmake -S . -B build -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Debug     # configure once.
cmake --build build                               # rebuilds only what changed (incl. headers).
ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure        # run the tests.
```

| Keyword | Applies to |
|---|---|
| PRIVATE. | this target only. |
| PUBLIC. | this target and everything linking it. |
| INTERFACE. | only targets linking it. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why avoid set(CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS ...) scattered around?", "answer": "It's global and mutable: every target after that line changes, and the order of lines matters. Per-target settings make each target's configuration explicit and local."}
```

examples.title: A header change that rebuilds everything it should
examples.situation: A changed class header recompiles every dependent translation unit before tests link against one consistent layout.
walkthrough: **A changed class header:** a field is added to Order in include/order.h.
**Recompiles every dependent translation unit:** cmake --build rebuilds order.cpp, parse.cpp, main.cpp and test_parse.cpp.
**Before tests link against one consistent layout:** ctest will run against objects that all agree on Order's size.
examples.result: No stale object uses an old layout, and every target shares one standard.

examples.title: The global flag surprise
examples.situation: A CMakeLists sets CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS to -O0 near the end "for debugging", and a colleague's library later in the file silently loses its optimisation settings.
walkthrough: Global variables affect everything defined after them.
Use CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE for debug vs release.
Put target-specific options on the target with target_compile_options.
examples.result: Each target's settings are visible where the target is defined.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Object files built with any compiler flags can be mixed safely as long as the linker accepts their names.
misconceptions.correction: Different standards, defines or ABI flags can change class layouts and inline definitions. The linker only matches names, so mismatches cause silent ODR violations.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, why did the std::string member read garbage?

analogy.example: A CMake project is like **a kitchen with labelled recipe cards per dish** (targets). Each card lists its own ingredients and methods. A **global note taped to the fridge** ("everything extra salty") affects every dish made afterwards, and dishes made with different measuring systems (standards and flags) don't fit together on one plate.
limitations: Kitchens forgive; linkers don't check layouts.
PUBLIC settings are ingredients the next dish inherits.

remediation.explanation: For each setting ask: **which target needs it, and should targets that link it inherit it (PUBLIC) or not (PRIVATE)?** Never mix objects from different configurations.

recap.summary: To configure a multi-target CMake project, describe each library, executable and test as a target, attach standards, include directories, options and links per target with PRIVATE, PUBLIC or INTERFACE scope instead of global flags, keep one consistent standard and ABI across the program, and let CMake rebuild everything that depends on a changed header.
